ref: Scholarship: George Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae, Eng. transl. p.172 (Bull on Haer. 4.20.1 'His own hands'); Bull's own note cites iv. 20. 1
greek: Against them the holy bishop, everywhere in his writings, affirms and proves these two points; First, that this world was in no wise created by inferior powers, alien from the essence and nature of the Most High God; but was made by the Most High God Himself, through “His own offspring”, and through “His own hands”, (to use the very words of Irenzeus,) that is to say, through the Son and the Holy Ghost.
greek_edition: English (source is English). Read from archive.org djvu OCR; OCR writes 'Irenzeus' for Irenaeus. Bull's Latin notes sit in the same pages.

what_it_says: Bull reads Irenaeus as saying God made the world through his own offspring and his own hands, that is, through the Son and the Holy Ghost.
limits: Bull is a 17th-century Nicene apologist, not a neutral reader; the 'hands = Son and Spirit' reading is his gloss plus Irenaeus's own words; Irenaeus's phrase 'His own hands' is in Haer. 4.20.1 per Bull's footnote; not checked against Harvey.

ref: Scholarship: Bull, Defensio, p.172 answering the angels-as-ministers passage (Bull's Latin note '[c. 30, 9. p. 163.]'; the brief lists this as Haer. 2.30.9)
greek: I reply, that Irenæus does not there mean, (as the Arians would have it,) a minister extraneous to the Father, but of one substance and of the selfsame nature with Him; or rather he merely meant, that God the Father accomplished that work of creation through the Son and the Holy Ghost, which the heretics used to attribute to ministering angels or inferior powers.

what_it_says: Bull answers the 'minister' objection: Irenaeus's ministry of Son and Spirit is of one substance with the Father, not an extraneous servant.
limits: Bull's answer is an argument from Irenaeus's wider usage; Bull does not exclude that Irenaeus's wording is subordinationist in a sense Nicaea later rejected; Irenaeus's exact Greek behind 'minister' not checked.

ref: Scholarship: Bull, Defensio, p.174 summarising Haer. 4 (Father, Son, Holy Ghost, 'Wisdom'); Bull cites iv. 20. 1 and v. 1, 28 in notes on p.173-174
greek: In these passages Irenæus asserts such an identity of essence (saving always the distinction of persons) between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, (whom with Theophilus of Antioch and others, he designates under the name of Wisdom,) as to say, that the Father, in creating the world through the Son and the Holy Ghost, made it through His own self.

limits: Bull's claim 'Irenaeus asserts such an identity of essence' is Bull's interpretation; whether Irenaeus's Greek or Latin uses an 'essence' term here was not checked; the naming of Son and Spirit as 'Wisdom' is contested (see I10 notes).

Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; IPSE A SEMETIPSO substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens.

ref: Scholarship: Bethune-Baker, Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, ch. VII 'The Logos Doctrine', Irenaeus section, p.130

They are a mystery. The Father is God revealing Himself; the Son is God revealed. The Father is the invisible of the Son, while the Son is the [p.131] visible of the Father.

And because he was being drawn away by the error of Valentinus, Irenæus wrote his work On the Ogdoad, in which he shows that he himself had been acquainted with the first successors of the apostles.

Afterwards John, the disciple of the Lord, who also reclined on his bosom, published his Gospel, while staying at Ephesus in Asia.

We have requested our brother and comrade Irenæus to carry this letter to you, and we ask you to hold him in esteem, as zealous for the covenant of Christ.”
